subject: Surgical Triads
title: Trauma & Orthopedic Triads
preview: Trauma patterns combine orthopedic injury, fat embolism and the physiologic lethal triad of major hemorrhage.

sections.title: The classic unhappy triad
points: A valgus force to a planted knee can injure the ACL, MCL and meniscus.
The historical description names the medial meniscus, while acute-injury series often identify lateral meniscal tears; imaging and examination establish the actual injury.

sections.title: Fat embolism syndrome
points: Respiratory distress or hypoxemia, confusion or altered consciousness, and a petechial rash are classic clues.
Onset and severity vary; a normal initial examination does not eliminate subsequent concern after high-risk fracture.

sections.title: Trauma lethal triad
points: Remember hypothermia + acidosis + coagulopathy as mutually reinforcing dangers in major bleeding.
Damage-control resuscitation seeks hemorrhage control, warming and correction of physiologic derangements.

sections.title: Exam trap
points: Do not equate any knee injury with all components of the classic triad.
Persistent severe pain on passive stretch after trauma warrants consideration of compartment syndrome.

quickRevision: The classical unhappy triad describes ACL, MCL and meniscal injury after knee trauma.
Fat embolism syndrome can produce respiratory dysfunction, neurological findings and petechial rash after trauma.
The lethal triad of major trauma is hypothermia, coagulopathy and acidosis.

quiz.question: In acute compartment syndrome, what is an early concerning symptom?
options: Normal muscle tension after major trauma
quiz.explanation: Marked pain during passive stretch after fracture or trauma is an early warning of compartment syndrome; distal pulses can remain intact.
